purpose: Lactulose is mainly used to treat constipation by helping you have softer, easier bowel movements. It is also used in people with liver disease to help remove a harmful substance called ammonia from the body, which can affect brain function if it builds up too much.
how_it_works: Lactulose is a sugar that your body cannot digest or absorb. It draws water into your intestines, which softens your stool and helps move things along. In people with liver problems, it also pulls ammonia into the gut so it can be passed out of your body in your stool.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects are gas, bloating, stomach cramps, and diarrhea, especially when you first start taking it. These often get better as your body adjusts. Diarrhea that is severe or ongoing should be reported to your doctor.
warnings: If you have diabetes, be aware that lactulose contains sugars and may affect your blood sugar levels. Do not use it if you are on a galactose-restricted diet. Overuse can cause low potassium or sodium levels in your blood, so take only the amount your doctor recommends. Tell your doctor if you need to have a colonoscopy, as lactulose may need to be stopped beforehand.
typical_dosing: For constipation in adults, the usual dose is 15 to 30 mL (1 to 2 tablespoons) by mouth once a day, and it may be increased if needed. For liver-related ammonia problems, doses can be higher and more frequent — often 3 to 4 times a day — as directed by your doctor. It may take 24 to 48 hours to work for constipation.
